title: Teach a small model when an empty form field is for a signature
summary: An empty signature line and an ordinary text field can look almost identical. The clue is often beside the field: its label, neighbouring date field or place in the form.
audience: A researcher developing local document-processing models for digitised forms.
why_it_matters: An empty signature line and an ordinary text field can look almost identical. The clue is often beside the field: its label, neighbouring date field or place in the form.
proposed_fix: Train from scratch a small shared CNN with two views: field crop and an expanded context crop with the field location marked. Fuse the embeddings with relative geometry; compare simple concatenation against a learned gate. Use 96–128 pixel crops and a target below one million parameters. No LLM or paid model calls. Class-balanced minibatches and a contrastive/margin term for confusing signature/text pairs. Keep loss weighting, context radius and feature fusion as separately tested factors. Primary endpoint is conditional field-type classification using provided boxes. Add deterministic line/rectangle candidates as a secondary operational test only after measuring their proposal recall; never report oracle-box accuracy as detector accuracy.
example: A form contains two blank underlined regions. One is a postal address and one is a signature. A crop of the blank line alone loses the information needed to tell them apart.
question: Can nearby words and layout help a small model distinguish signature fields from ordinary text boxes?
flow: Use public forms with labelled text and signature fields.
Train small models with different amounts of surrounding context.
Test on separate form families and compare costly mistakes.
deliverable: A trained compact context model, a reproducible test of which surrounding evidence matters, and an explicit account of accuracy versus CPU cost. This is field-type recognition given candidate regions, not a claim to solve complete document extraction.
contribution: A task-specific trained model and falsifiable explanation of when local relational context helps rare form fields under a fixed resource budget. A negative result remains useful if the controlled comparison is sound.

title: Keep marginal notes separate when manuscript training labels are rough
summary: A digitisation model must separate main text from marginal notes. Precise pixel labels are expensive; coarse boundaries can teach a model to erase small notes or merge them into the main text.
audience: A researcher developing manuscript digitisation models without precise new annotations.
why_it_matters: A digitisation model must separate main text from marginal notes. Precise pixel labels are expensive; coarse boundaries can teach a model to erase small notes or merge them into the main text.
proposed_fix: Train a compact L-U-Net-inspired or narrow U-Net from scratch using 256x256 tiles, with main text/comment/decoration/background targets. A roughly 65k-parameter L-U-Net is described in the closest weak-label paper; the actual implementation and parameter count must be checked. Create controlled label approximations only in training: polygon simplification and class-wise erosion/dilation with a fixed scale normalised by page resolution. Assign boundary pixels a set of plausible adjacent classes, preserve confident interior supervision, and add consistency between two image perturbations. Compare set-valued boundary loss with simply ignoring the same band, matched soft-label smoothing, and hard noisy masks. Do not mix boundary noise with missing-whole-region labels in the primary experiment. Optional missing-note stress test is separately reported. Synthetic coarsening measures tolerance to specified label defects. It does not prove human annotation-time savings, expert disagreement or restoration of historically correct text. Construct uncertain boundary bands and plausible classes solely from coarsened training labels. Keep clean source masks hidden from the weak-label learner; a separately labelled clean-supervision oracle may be reported as an upper reference, never an equal-information baseline.
example: A narrow handwritten comment touches the main text. Enlarging its training mask by a few pixels may swallow surrounding strokes; an ordinary segmentation loss then treats this approximation as unquestionable truth.
question: Can a model learn to keep handwritten margin notes separate when its training outlines are imperfect?
flow: Use public manuscript pages and create controlled rough training outlines.
Train a small model that can tolerate uncertain boundaries.
Check untouched labels in a different manuscript for lost margin notes.

title: Let a small earthquake detector admit when its timing is unreliable
summary: A small model may put a precise-looking timestamp on noise or on a poorly defined arrival.
audience: A researcher preparing seismic phase picks for later analysis.
why_it_matters: A small model may put a precise-looking timestamp on noise or on a poorly defined arrival.
proposed_fix: Train a small 1-D phase-picking CNN with quality-weighted/soft arrival targets and a confidence head. Use handcrafted onset features plus a boosted model as a strong low-cost alternative. Pretrained PhaseNet weights are optional only after their exact release/licence and training exposure are verified.
example: A trace has a weak first arrival. Returning a broad uncertain interval may be more honest than a timestamp that is wrong by half a second.
question: Can a small model tell us when it is unsure about an earthquake signal's arrival time?
flow: Use public earthquake signals and real noise recordings.
Train a small model to locate arrivals and express uncertainty.
Test timing mistakes on separate events and stations.
deliverable: A compact picker, controlled label-quality ablations and uncertainty/false-pick evaluation on public traces.
contribution: Study the reliability/coverage trade-off with imperfect labels and real noise, not simply compress a phase picker.
